facts.text: The credibility of a simulation is the degree to which a decision maker can trust its results enough to act on them; credibility is earned with evidence rather than realistic-looking pictures.
facts.quote: The credibility of a simulation is the degree to which a decision maker can trust its results enough to act on them, and it is earned with evidence, not with realistic-looking pictures.

facts.text: Visual plausibility is weak evidence of simulation credibility because a simulation can be visually convincing and physically wrong at the same time.
facts.quote: "It looks right" is weak evidence, because a simulation can be visually convincing and physically wrong at the same time.

facts.text: Assessing simulation credibility requires examining the decision being supported, the consequences of a wrong decision, program error checks, comparisons with real-machine measurements under relevant conditions, remaining uncertainty, independent review, and the limits of the evidence.
facts.quote: What exactly is the simulation being used to decide? How bad would a wrong decision be? Has the program been checked for errors?

facts.text: The industries examined by the booklet—space flight, medical devices, nuclear power, aviation, rail and road vehicles—ask the same simulation-credibility questions in different words.
facts.quote: Every industry the booklet examined, from space flight to medical devices, nuclear power, aviation, rail and road vehicles, asks these same questions in different words [Chapter 10].

facts.text: Simulation credibility applies to a specific combination of model version, inputs, supported decision and range of conditions.
facts.quote: Credibility belongs to a combination: this version of this model, with these inputs, for this decision, inside this range of conditions.

facts.text: No commercial simulation package, open-source simulator or digital twin is credible on its own.
facts.quote: No commercial package, open-source simulator or digital twin is credible on its own.

facts.text: The space agency standard refuses to combine simulation credibility factors into a single score because a high mark in one area can conceal weak validation in another.
facts.quote: the space agency standard refuses to add its credibility factors into a single score, because a high mark in one area can hide a weak validation in another [Chapter 10].

facts.text: In the passage's example, a simulated haul truck stopping distance of 42 m from 30 km/h on a wet ramp is credible for a braking decision only if the brake model has been compared with real stops on a similar truck, surface and speed.
facts.quote: a simulated haul truck stops in 42 m from 30 km/h on a wet ramp. That number is credible for a braking decision only if the brake model was compared with real stops on a similar truck, surface and speed

facts.text: In the simulated haul-truck braking example, the measured disagreement with real stops plus the remaining uncertainty must be smaller than the safety margin required by the braking decision.
facts.quote: the measured disagreement plus the remaining uncertainty is smaller than the safety margin the decision needs.

facts.text: The manufacturer has never used simulation as safety evidence.
facts.quote: The manufacturer has never used simulation as safety evidence

facts.text: The booklet's hostile review ranks the objection that the simulator has not earned the right to replace physical evidence as the strongest objection to the plan.
facts.quote: the booklet's hostile review ranks "the simulator has not earned the right to replace physical evidence" as the strongest objection to the plan [Chapter 13].

facts.text: Simulation credibility work must be finished before the prototype arrives in mid-2027; otherwise, the four-month validation window becomes the first attempt at simulation methodology rather than a confirmation campaign.
facts.quote: Credibility work must be finished before the prototype arrives in mid-2027, or the four-month window becomes the first attempt at simulation methodology rather than a confirmation campaign [Chapter 10].
